title: Interest rates on hold but RBA governor keeps door open to hikes

Topic:Interest Rates

The RBA Monetary Policy Board has voted to keep the cash rate at 4.35 per cent. (AAP: Bianca De Marchi)

The RBA has kept interest rates at 4.35 per cent.

Headline inflation cooled a bit in June, and property prices have declined by a little more than anticipated, but underlying inflation pressures remain elevated.

The monetary policy board's next interest rate meeting will be held on September 28-29.

The Reserve Bank has kept interest rates on hold at 4.35 per cent, in a unanimous decision.

The move comes after headline inflation cooled a bit in June, and property prices declined by a little more than anticipated in recent months.

It also comes after economists have been warning that underlying inflation is still too high, with some saying that they expect interest rates to have to rise again, at some point, to squeeze inflation out of the economy.

But the RBA's latest forecasts, also released today, show a more upbeat picture than the bank's last forecasts published in May.

They suggest inflation may have peaked a lot lower than the RBA previously feared.

However, Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock used her press conference to highlight that the risks to inflation remain to the upside, including the Middle East conflict.

Michele Bullock says the RBA board discussed whether to hold or hike rates in August. (AAP: Dan Himbrechts)

Asked if the board considered cutting rates, Ms Bullock said it only considered the options of hiking interest rates or holding them steady, eventually deciding unanimously on the latter.

"There was a diversity of views [on the board] about how strongly people felt they were worried about inflation, but everyone was at least a little bit worried about what those inflationary risks may be and what they may imply," she said.

"We're staying put, but staying put with a very clear focus on watching how the data come in, and whether or not the next interest rate move, we may need to increase again, if it looks like we're not on track to get inflation back down."

In the central bank's new forecasts, headline inflation, while still well above the bank's 2-3 per cent target range, has come in nearly a full percentage point lower than its previous forecast.

Australia's economy grew at an annual rate of 2.5 per cent in the March quarter, the same as in the previous quarter.

Its preferred more stable measure of "trimmed mean" inflation is 0.2 per cent below the last forecast.

The bank is now forecasting inflation to have a slower, steadier trajectory down from current levels to be back at the 2.5 per cent midpoint of its target by early 2028.

Following today's decision, the official cash rate target will remain at 4.35 per cent for the next seven weeks, until the RBA Board's next meeting in late September.

Its latest forecasts are based on an assumption that the cash rate stays around current levels at 4.35 per cent in December 2028, versus the previous forecasts which had the cash rate peaking around 4.7 per cent over the next year.

That does not mean that the Reserve Bank itself expects rates to be on hold at current levels for the next two years or more; it is based on what traders are betting on in financial markets.

But the fact that both headline and "core" inflation are still expected to get back to the mid-point of the RBA's 2-3 per cent target range by early 2028, despite one less rate cut than the May forecasts, is evidence of the lower-than-feared inflation trajectory and suggests that the RBA may be done with rate hikes, if its forecasts prove accurate.

The bank's new forecasts show that many borrowers have also had the edge taken off recent interest rate rises by competition between the banks for mortgages.

"Spreads between lending rates and the cash rate also remain low by historical standards, reflecting low risk premia, favourable funding conditions and strong competition in lending markets," the RBA noted.

Australia's property market has entered a downturn after both house and unit prices fell for the first time in more than three years, bringing an end to the recent housing boom.

Despite this, the RBA has noted that scheduled mortgage repayments relative to household disposable income have increased to be close to their 2024 peak.

It says Australian households are spending about 12 per cent of their disposable income servicing debt, including consumer credit repayments. That overall number includes the millions of households that have little or no debt.

As in 2024, Australia is now approaching the overall debt payment burden households faced just before the global financial crisis in 2008, when the RBA's cash rate was 7.25 per cent, but mortgage debts were generally much smaller.

However, the RBA has noted that the previous period of low interest rates had seen most mortgage borrowers stash extra cash into their offset accounts or get ahead on their loan repayments and build large redraw buffers, with the typical borrower now having the buffer of around a year's worth of scheduled repayments in these savings.
